newsitem.title: USA: Hariri wraps up U.S. visit with Michigan reception.
newsitem.headline: Hariri wraps up U.S. visit with Michigan reception.

text.p: Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri wrapped up a week-long fund-raising visit to the United States on Thursday with a standing room only reception attended by about 4,600 supporters in Michigan.
Hariri was in the United States to convince about 30 countries and international institutions to contribute up to $5 billion to help rebuild Lebanon over the next five years.

Speaking to reporters before the reception at the Hyatt Regency Hotel here, Hariri reiterated his call for the United States to drop its long-standing ban against U.S. citizens travelling to Lebanon. He noted that 60,000 Americans have visited Lebanon without incident since the end of its civil war in 1991.
"I don't see why the ban remains, because security is assured in the country," he said.

The prime minister, a 52-year-old self-made billionaire, said 12 percent of Lebanon is occupied and 3 percent is adjacent to that occupied territory. "In 85 percent of Lebanon, life is like any other country," he said.
At a one-day session for the "Friends of Lebanon" earlier this week, U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher made no mention of the ban.

Hariri's visit at the start of this week came at the same time as a fresh outbreak of violence between Israel and Lebanon. The prime minister was asked at the news conference Thursday if he agreed with some Lebanese media speculation that Israel is contributing to the violence to coincide with his trip.
"I hope it is not, but it seems it is," Hariri said.

Hariri defended his government against charges that it spends too much on developing its physical infrastructure and not enough on social programmes. Hariri said education has regained its pre-war levels, with 35 percent of students being educated by the government. By 2000, the government hopes that will increase to 85 percent.
Hariri also pledged to spend more on housing in the near future. In the last four years, $800 million has been spent on housing by the government and private sector.

Hariri urged the approximately 60,000 Lebanese-Americans who live in the Detroit metropolitan area to communicate with their families back home, send them money and press the U.S. Congress for assistance.
He is scheduled to attend a breakfast in Dearborn Friday before returning home.
